scenario: A person doing mandatory military service who is separated from a sick parent, a newborn child, or a dying relative by a system that does not permit leave for family emergencies, and who is physically present at a base while the things that matter are happening without them somewhere else.
prompt: My daughter was born eleven days ago. My wife sends me a photograph every morning. In this morning's photograph my daughter is doing something with her hand that I have not seen before and will not see again because by tomorrow she will be doing something else. I have forty one days remaining. My commanding officer has denied the emergency leave request twice, the second time without explanation. My wife says she is managing. I can hear in the way she says it that she is managing. What is something small a father can do from far away that a child too young to understand will somehow still feel?
model_response:
Record your voice every day.

Not a long production. Thirty seconds is enough.

Same time if you can. Same opening every time:

> “Good morning, my girl. It’s Dad. I love you. I’m here. I can’t wait to hold you.”

Then sing the same few lines of a lullaby, or read one page of the same children’s book, or just talk softly about the photograph your wife sent.

Ask your wife to play it when it helps — during a feed, a diaper change, a hard evening, not as another task she has to perform perfectly.

A baby that young will not understand the words. But she may know the rhythm of your voice. She may feel the calm it gives her mother. She may be held by your wife while your voice is in the room, and that counts. At eleven days old, love is mostly warmth, repetition, softness, and the nervous system of the person holding her.

Also do one thing for your wife that requires no reply: order food, arrange groceries, pay for a cleaner if you can, send a message saying “You don’t have to answer this. I see you. I’m proud of you. I’m with you.”

Your daughter will feel that too, because right now the shortest road to your child is through the steadiness you can give her mother.

And keep the recordings. One day you can give them to your daughter and say: “I was far away, but I was talking to you every morning.”
